# Detection placement comparison (simulated)

**SIMULATED from a simplified, uncalibrated fire-spread model; not a prediction of real fires or real detection times.** Generated by `python -m detection.run`; the same numbers are in `results.json`.

## Question

Four sensor masts go on 16 candidate sites in a 20 x 20 cell (10 km x 10 km) window of Khao Yai National Park. Does choosing the sites by simulated time to detection give a different placement from choosing them by where fires have started, and how do both compare with the placement the project already uses?

## Method

- Fire grid: the real 40 x 40 region (500 m cells, land cover and elevation from the project data). The sensor window sits at row 15, column 3 of the region. Ignitions are drawn only inside the window, with probability proportional to smoothed 2012 to 2025 satellite fire counts; fire then spreads over the whole region, so it can leave and re-enter the window.
- Spread: minimum-travel-time model on an 8-neighbour grid with hand-set fuel, slope and wind multipliers (`detection/fire_sim.py`). One wind value per scenario, drawn from daytime hours of the fire-season record.
- Scenarios: 4,000 TRAIN scenarios (seed 101) choose placements and 4,000 independent TEST scenarios (seed 202) produce every number below.
- Detection: a sensor detects the fire the moment it enters any cell it sees. The satellite detects every fire `baseline` hours after ignition. A scenario's detection time is the earlier of the two.
- Placements compared, all with 4 sensors and all scored by the same function on TEST:
  - Satellite only: no sensors.
  - Current placement: the dashboard's placement, which maximises hazard x value coverage and equals the exact optimum of that objective.
  - Fire-history coverage: the 4 sites that see the largest total ignition weight, with no spread model. Solved by brute force over all 1,820 subsets.
  - Time-to-detection, greedy: greedy maximisation of expected hours saved on TRAIN.
  - Time-to-detection, exact: integer programme (CBC, 120 s limit) on TRAIN. The true optimum was also found by brute force over all subsets as a check.

- Fire-history coverage minus current placement: -1.063 h (95% interval -1.150 to -0.982)
- Time-to-detection exact minus fire-history coverage: +0.000 h (95% interval +0.000 to +0.000)

Exact solver on TRAIN: proven optimal = True (status Optimal, within the 120 s limit); its value matches the brute-force optimum over all subsets. Greedy also found that optimum.

## Finding

In all 20 settings the time-to-detection optimum is the same four sites as the fire-history coverage optimum (sites 6, 7, 9, 10). Fires that start inside a seen cell supply 76.8% or more of the optimum's saving at every setting (fires detected after spreading supply 0.0% to 23.2%). So in this simulation the time-to-detection objective reduces to coverage weighted by where fires have started, and the spread model changes nothing about which sites are chosen.

The choice is not always clear-cut: at the headline setting the second-best set on TRAIN (6, 7, 8, 10) is 0.019 h behind the best. A different random TRAIN draw can put a near-tied set on top, so the equality above holds for these 4,000 scenarios and is not a guarantee.

## Caveats

- The current placement was optimised for hazard x value, which includes what is worth protecting. The other three placements optimise detection of ignitions only. That the current placement saves fewer simulated hours here does not make it the worse placement, and this comparison declares no winner.
- The fire-history and time-to-detection placements are chosen and scored on fires drawn from the same fire-history distribution. That is circular in the same way as the hazard layer, whose fire-density term comes from the same detections. TRAIN and TEST separate only the random scenarios, not the ignition distribution or the model.
- Spread rates come from experimental burns in deciduous forest elsewhere in Thailand; Khao Yai is mostly evergreen and no rate was found for it. The 6 m/min end of the sensitivity range has no source checked.
- Instant detection on entering a visible cell makes the numbers more favourable to sensors than real detection would be. The fixed satellite delay, the single wind value for the whole map and the unfitted spread model have an unknown effect on the comparison.
- Viewsheds exist only for the 20 x 20 window, so a sensor near the window edge is not credited with cells it would see outside it. This works against sensors.
- The sensitivity settings reuse the same TRAIN and TEST seeds, so the ignition and wind draws are the same in every setting. The 20 settings are not 20 independent confirmations, and a near-tie between sites breaks the same way each time.
- Differences between placements that sit within the bootstrap interval are not distinguishable at this number of scenarios.
